parole.testo: First attested in the 16th century. Borrowed from Middle Dutch almanag (Flanders 1426), from Medieval Latin almanach (1267), from Andalusian Arabic الْمَنَاخ (al-manāḵ, “calendar”). The Ibero-Arabic term is of uncertain origin. See also almanaque. Perhaps originally derived from Byzantine Greek ἀλμε
From Middle High German barke, borrowed via Middle Dutch barke from Middle French barque, from Old French barque, from Late Latin barca.

Ultimately onomatopoeic. Attested 15th century in the sense “to wail with pain”, compare also Alemannic German blaffe (“to chatter”). The sense “to bark” is more northern, possibly borrowed from Middle Dutch blaffen (1350), whence also obsolete English blaff. Compare bellen, kläffen.
Dialectal variant of Doppel, from Middle Dutch dubbel, dobbel, from French double.
From Middle High German vloite and variants; borrowed via Middle Dutch floite from Old French fleüte.
From (late) Middle High German franze, which is borrowed via Middle Dutch from Old French frenge.
Diminutive of an obsolete simplex frett, which is borrowed via Middle Dutch furet, fret from Old French furet, + -chen. Compare modern Dutch fret.

parole.significato: farm, farmstead, of any size, but especially a small one
parole.testo: From Middle High German gehüfte, so attested 1309 in Königsdorf near Cologne; later also in East Central German gehoffte (and variants). Collective formation from Hof (“yard, farmyard, farm”). Regarding the Dutch colonisation in the east, it is possible that the German word goes back to Middle Dutch

From Middle High German hübesch (“courtly”), from the root of modern Hof (“court”). Cognate with Yiddish היפּש (hipsh). The term was probably borrowed into written Middle High German from Middle Dutch hovesch via West Central German, in which process the Central German -v- was hypercorrectly replace
From late Middle Dutch jueel and its modern continuation in Dutch juweel. The Dutch word is borrowed from Old French jouel.
From Middle Dutch cant, cante (“edge, rim, piece of bread”), adopted from Dutch settlers in East Elbia since the 12th century. Compare synonymous German Kante.

parole.significato: to nought, to nullify, to quash, to cassate
parole.testo: From Middle High German kassieren (West Central German, 14th c.), probably from Middle Dutch casseren (13th c.), from Old French casser, quasser (“to annul”). Ultimately from a merger of Latin cassāre and quassāre. The German may later have been reinforced also by Italian cassare, from the same Lati

From Middle High German kástel (“fortified castle, city”), from Old High German kastel, and its doublet Middle High German kastḗl (“castle”), from Middle Dutch casteel, from Picardian Old French castel. Both ultimately from Latin castellum, which also directly influenced the modern form and sense.

parole.significato: a case; a suitcase or briefcase
parole.testo: From Late Middle High German koffer, from Middle Dutch coffer, from Old French cofre.

parole.significato: madder (Rubia tinctorum) and the pigment from it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Dutch crappe, from Proto-Germanic *krappô (“hook”), a reference to the plant’s hook-shaped thorns. Doublet of Krapfen.

Uncertain, in spite of being the present Standard Dutch term for the daisy, madelief n, which originally was feminine as well, madelieve f. Theoretized to be borrowed from Middle Dutch matelieve f, though this is difficult in view of the term's presence in Austria.

From Late Middle High German mēwe (Strasbourg, 1449), borrowed from Middle Dutch mêwe (along the Rhine) and Middle Low German mêwe (in East Prussia and along the Elbe), both from Proto-West Germanic *maiwā, from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz, which see. From Middle Dutch net (“neat, decent, pretty”), from Old French net (“neat, decent”), from Latin nitidus. Compare English neat.

parole.significato: park (piece of ground in or near a city or town, enclosed and kept for ornament and recreation)
parole.testo: A doublet of inherited Pferch (“pen [for animals]”). The form Park was first borrowed in the 15th/16th centuries from Middle Dutch park, in which the word had developed the sense “recreation park, enclosed hunting grounds” under the influence of Old French parc. Inherited from Middle High German pastēde, likely from Middle Dutch pasteide, from Old French pasté, from Late Latin pasta (“paste, dough, pastry cake”). See there for more. Cognate with Hunsrik Pasdet.
From Late Middle High German baviān (15th c.), from Middle Dutch baviaen (cf. Modern Dutch baviaan), from older baubijn, from Middle French babouin.

From Middle High German pieke, from Middle Dutch pike, from Old Dutch *pīk, from Proto-West Germanic *pīk. Already in Dutch the word was influenced by French pic (“tip”). Another influence is German Picke (“pick, pickaxe”), from picken. The precise relation between all of these words is uncertain.
From Pott + Wal, a calque of Middle Dutch potswal, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz + *hwalaz.

parole.significato: princess (female member of a royal family other than a queen, especially a daughter or granddaughter)
parole.testo: From Prinzess(e) (“princess”) + -in (redundant female suffix). The former through Middle Dutch princesse from Old French princesse.

parole.significato: defined area of land, principally used for hunting or foraging
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German riviere (“undeveloped area; hunting ground; river”), borrowed, probably through Middle Dutch riviere (“river; riverside used for hunting birds”), from Old French riviere (“idem”), from Latin riparia (“riverside”). Cognate with modern Dutch rivier, English river, mod

From Middle High German ritter, from Middle Dutch ridder, Flemish byform of rîder, from rîden + -er (equivalent to German reiten + -er). In Middle High German, both ritter and rīter (whence modern Reiter) were used in the sense of “horseman”, “mounted man-at-arms”, as well as for the (emerging) rank

From Middle High German tanz, from Middle Dutch dans, from Old French danse, dancier, equivalent to a deverbal from tanzen. See tanzen for more.
From north-western Middle High German taxieren (14th c.), from Middle Dutch taxeren (13th c.), from Latin taxāre.

From Middle Dutch terpentijn, from Old French terbentine, turbentine, Latin terebinthīna, from terebintha, from Ancient Greek τερεβινθίνη (terebinthínē), from τερεβινθινος (terebinthinos), from τερέβινθος (terébinthos). See also turpentine.

parole.significato: bar (table or board in a pub or restaurant)
parole.testo: Originally “cupboard, safe for the cash box”. From Low Franconian and West Central German dialects (attested early 16th century), probably through Middle Dutch teke (compare dated modern Dutch teek), from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē). The word was introduced into modern standard Germ

Formally continuing Middle High German verītelen (“to become weak, insipid”, a 14th-c. hapax). By surface analysis, eitel (“vain”) + ver- -en. parole.significato: fleece (wool of a sheep or similar animal, with or without the skin)
parole.testo: 16th century, at first only in reference to the Order of the Golden Fleece, from Middle Dutch vlies, from Proto-West Germanic *fleus. Borrowed from Middle Dutch wafel. Cognate with Dutch wafel, English waffle and English wafer, Swedish våffla, Icelandic vafla.
From Middle Dutch want, gewant, from Old Dutch *giwant, from Proto-Germanic *gawandą, from the root of winden.

From Middle Dutch tīdinge, whence is borrowed Middle High German zīdunge (West Central German), from Proto-West Germanic *tīdungu (“message”), from the verb *tīdōn (“to happen”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi (“time, interval”). From this the later Upper German form zītunge, and then the modern for

From rare Middle High German zwist (Ripuarian, 14th c.), borrowed from Middle Dutch twist, from Proto-West Germanic *twist, from Proto-Germanic *twistaz (whence also English twist). Later reinforced by cognate Low German Twist, from Middle Low German twist, twest. Since ca. 1700 in regular standard

parole.testo: Uncertain, perhaps borrowed from Middle Dutch focken (“to breed; to fuck; to tease”) with uncommon sound development of [k] to [p] (influenced either by the preceding rounded vowel or assimilation to the /f/), from Old Dutch *fokkon, from Proto-West Germanic *fukkōn, possibly from Proto-Germanic *fu

Early 18th century. Either directly from modern French graver or through Dutch and Middle Dutch graveren (13th c.), from Old French graver, from Frankish *graban, from Proto-Germanic *grabaną. Doublet of graben.

Borrowed from Low German laff, which is either inherited from Middle Low German *laf (seemingly not attested) or borrowed from Middle Dutch laf (early 15th century), all probably from Proto-Germanic *laba-, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Compare modern Dutch laf (“cowardly”).
